question.en: A `Car` class starts small. Over six months it grows methods to compute fuel efficiency, save itself to disk, print itself to the screen, and serialize to JSON. Every new feature edits this one class, and every edit risks breaking an unrelated feature. What design rule is being broken?
question.ro: O clasa `Car` incepe mica. In sase luni capata metode care calculeaza eficienta combustibilului, se salveaza pe disc, se afiseaza pe ecran si se serializeaza in JSON. Fiecare functionalitate noua modifica aceasta clasa, iar fiecare modificare risca sa strice o functionalitate fara legatura. Ce regula de proiectare este incalcata?

answer.en: The Single Responsibility Principle — a class should have only ONE reason to change. The `Car` above changes for storage reasons, for display reasons, for calculation reasons. SOLID, and SRP first, is the topic of this step.
answer.ro: Principiul Responsabilitatii Unice — o clasa ar trebui sa aiba un SINGUR motiv sa se schimbe. `Car` de mai sus se schimba din motive de stocare, de afisare, de calcul. SOLID, si SRP in primul rand, este tema acestui pas.

content.en: **SOLID** is a set of five design principles for writing object-oriented code that stays maintainable as it grows. They were popularised by Robert C. Martin. None of them is enforced by the compiler — they are discipline, not syntax. The payoff is code that is **loosely coupled**, easy to test, and cheap to extend.
content.ro: **SOLID** este un set de cinci principii de proiectare pentru a scrie cod orientat pe obiecte care ramane mentenabil pe masura ce creste. Au fost popularizate de Robert C. Martin. Niciunul nu este impus de compilator — sunt disciplina, nu sintaxa. Castigul este cod **slab cuplat**, usor de testat si ieftin de extins.

content.en: A class should have only **one reason to change** — it should focus on a single responsibility. If you can describe a class only with the word "and" (it stores data AND saves it AND prints it), it likely has too many responsibilities.
content.ro: O clasa ar trebui sa aiba un singur **motiv sa se schimbe** — sa se concentreze pe o singura responsabilitate. Daca poti descrie o clasa doar folosind "si" (stocheaza date SI le salveaza SI le afiseaza), probabil are prea multe responsabilitati.

items.en: Easier to understand — each class tells one story.
items.ro: Mai usor de inteles — fiecare clasa spune o singura poveste.

items.en: Lower coupling between business logic and infrastructure.
items.ro: Cuplaj mai mic intre logica de business si infrastructura.

items.en: Improved testability and reusability — you can test the calculation without touching the disk.
items.ro: Testabilitate si reutilizare imbunatatite — poti testa calculul fara sa atingi discul.

content.ro: Iata o clasa `Car` care **incalca** SRP. Observa cate sarcini fara legatura si-a asumat:

content.en: These methods are not really about being a `Car`. The class has taken on four jobs at once: **managing state**, **computing efficiency**, **serialization support**, and **printing to screen**. A change in the file format and a change in the display logic would both force edits to the same class.
content.ro: Aceste metode nu tin cu adevarat de a fi un `Car`. Clasa si-a asumat patru sarcini deodata: **gestionarea starii**, **calculul eficientei**, **suportul de serializare** si **afisarea pe ecran**. O schimbare a formatului de fisier si o schimbare a logicii de afisare ar forta amandoua modificari in aceeasi clasa.

content.ro: Solutia: da fiecarei responsabilitati propria clasa. `Car` pastreaza doar starea; calculul, serializarea si afisarea se muta fiecare in afara:

question.en: Splitting one class into four means more files and more types to navigate. When is this split worth it, and when is it over-engineering?
question.ro: Impartirea unei clase in patru inseamna mai multe fisiere si mai multe tipuri de navigat. Cand merita aceasta impartire si cand este supra-inginerie?

answer.en: It is worth it when the responsibilities change for **different reasons or at different rates** — the file format evolves independently of the display, so coupling them creates friction. It is over-engineering when the "responsibilities" are tiny, always change together, and will never be reused or tested in isolation. SRP is about **reasons to change**, not about counting methods: a class with ten cohesive getters still has one responsibility.
answer.ro: Merita atunci cand responsabilitatile se schimba din **motive diferite sau in ritmuri diferite** — formatul de fisier evolueaza independent de afisare, deci cuplarea lor creeaza frictiune. Este supra-inginerie cand "responsabilitatile" sunt minuscule, se schimba mereu impreuna si nu vor fi niciodata reutilizate sau testate izolat. SRP tine de **motive de schimbare**, nu de numararea metodelor: o clasa cu zece getteri coezivi are tot o singura responsabilitate.

note.en: Course 12, section "SOLID Principles" (Prof. Gavrilut). SRP is the first of the five.
note.ro: Cursul 12, sectiunea "SOLID Principles" (Prof. Gavrilut). SRP este primul dintre cele cinci.

question.en: Your `area()` method is a big `switch` over a shape-type enum. The product team asks for a new `Triangle` shape. To add it, you must open the existing, already-tested `Shape` class and edit its `switch`. Why is being forced to edit tested code a design smell?
question.ro: Metoda ta `area()` este un `switch` mare peste un enum de tip de forma. Echipa de produs cere o forma noua `Triangle`. Ca sa o adaugi, trebuie sa deschizi clasa `Shape` existenta, deja testata, si sa-i modifici `switch`-ul. De ce este un miros de proiectare faptul ca esti obligat sa modifici cod deja testat?

answer.en: Every edit to working, tested code re-introduces the risk of breaking it — and forces re-testing of code that was already correct. The Open-Closed Principle says: you should be able to add the `Triangle` **without touching** `Shape` at all.
answer.ro: Fiecare modificare a unui cod functional si testat reintroduce riscul de a-l strica — si forteaza re-testarea unui cod care era deja corect. Principiul Deschis-Inchis spune: ar trebui sa poti adauga `Triangle` **fara sa atingi** deloc `Shape`.

content.en: "Software entities (modules, classes, functions) should be **open for extension but closed for modification**." You should be able to add new behaviour by writing new code, not by editing code that already works.
content.ro: "Entitatile software (module, clase, functii) ar trebui sa fie **deschise pentru extindere dar inchise pentru modificare**." Ar trebui sa poti adauga comportament nou scriind cod nou, nu modificand cod care deja functioneaza.

items.en: Reduces the risk of breaking existing, tested code.
items.ro: Reduce riscul de a strica cod existent, deja testat.

items.en: Easier to maintain — changes are additive.
items.ro: Mai usor de intretinut — schimbarile sunt aditive.

items.en: Natural support for plug-ins and third-party extensions.
items.ro: Suport natural pentru plug-in-uri si extensii din partea tertilor.

content.en:
**Two misconceptions to flag up front:**
1. **"Closed for modification" means I can never edit the class again.** No — it means stable code should not need editing **just to add a new variant**. Bug fixes are always allowed.
2. **OCP always means more abstraction.** Premature abstraction has its own cost. Apply OCP at the axis where you actually expect variation (new shapes), not everywhere.
content.ro:
**Doua conceptii gresite de semnalat de la inceput:**
1. **"Inchis pentru modificare" inseamna ca nu mai pot edita niciodata clasa.** Nu — inseamna ca un cod stabil nu ar trebui sa necesite editare **doar pentru a adauga o varianta noua**. Corectarea bug-urilor este mereu permisa.
2. **OCP inseamna mereu mai multa abstractizare.** Abstractizarea prematura are propriul cost. Aplica OCP pe axa unde chiar te astepti la variatie (forme noi), nu peste tot.

content.en: Here is a `Shape` that **breaks** OCP. The type is stored as an `enum`, and `area()` switches on it:
content.ro: Iata un `Shape` care **incalca** OCP. Tipul este stocat ca `enum`, iar `area()` face switch pe el:

content.en: To add a `Square`, you must edit the `enum` AND add a new `case` inside `area()`. You are modifying a class that already worked — exactly what OCP forbids.
content.ro: Ca sa adaugi un `Square`, trebuie sa modifici `enum`-ul SI sa adaugi un `case` nou in `area()`. Modifici o clasa care deja functiona — exact ce interzice OCP.

content.en: The fix uses **polymorphism**: make `Shape` an abstract base with a pure virtual `area()`. Each concrete shape is its own class. A new shape is a new class — no existing code is touched:
content.ro: Solutia foloseste **polimorfismul**: fa din `Shape` o baza abstracta cu un `area()` pur virtual. Fiecare forma concreta este propria clasa. O forma noua este o clasa noua — niciun cod existent nu este atins:

question.en: In the polymorphic version, adding `Square` means writing one new class and zero edits elsewhere. What language mechanism makes the existing code automatically "know" how to call `Square::area()` even though `Square` did not exist when that code was compiled?
question.ro: In varianta polimorfica, adaugarea lui `Square` inseamna scrierea unei singure clase noi si zero modificari in alta parte. Ce mecanism de limbaj face ca codul existent sa "stie" automat sa apeleze `Square::area()` desi `Square` nu exista cand a fost compilat acel cod?

answer.en: Dynamic dispatch through the **virtual table (VTable)**. Code that holds a `Shape*` calls `area()` indirectly through the object's vfptr — it resolves to whatever concrete type the object actually is at runtime. The caller is compiled against the **abstraction** (`Shape`), so a new derived type slots in with no recompilation of the caller. That indirection is exactly what makes the base "closed" while the hierarchy stays "open".
answer.ro: Dispatch dinamic prin **tabela virtuala (VTable)**. Codul care detine un `Shape*` apeleaza `area()` indirect prin vfptr-ul obiectului — se rezolva la tipul concret pe care obiectul il are de fapt la runtime. Apelantul este compilat fata de **abstractie** (`Shape`), deci un tip derivat nou se incadreaza fara recompilarea apelantului. Acea indirectare este exact ce face baza "inchisa" in timp ce ierarhia ramane "deschisa".

note.en: Course 12, section "SOLID Principles" — Open-Close Principle. Links back to virtual methods and the VTable (Course 5).
note.ro: Cursul 12, sectiunea "SOLID Principles" — Principiul Deschis-Inchis. Face legatura cu metodele virtuale si VTable (Cursul 5).

question.en: A function `void makeItFly(Bird& b)` calls `b.fly()`. It was written and tested against `Eagle`. Later, someone passes a `Penguin` — also a `Bird` by inheritance. The program now crashes. The function was never changed. Whose fault is the crash?
question.ro: O functie `void makeItFly(Bird& b)` apeleaza `b.fly()`. A fost scrisa si testata fata de `Eagle`. Mai tarziu, cineva trimite un `Penguin` — si el `Bird` prin mostenire. Programul crapa acum. Functia nu a fost niciodata modificata. A cui este vina crash-ului?

answer.en: The **hierarchy's** fault, not the function's. `Penguin` was declared a subtype of `Bird` but cannot honour the behaviour a `Bird` promises (it cannot fly). The Liskov Substitution Principle says a subtype must be usable **anywhere** the base type is expected — without surprises.
answer.ro: Vina **ierarhiei**, nu a functiei. `Penguin` a fost declarat subtip al lui `Bird` dar nu poate respecta comportamentul promis de `Bird` (nu poate zbura). Principiul Substitutiei Liskov spune ca un subtip trebuie sa fie utilizabil **oriunde** este asteptat tipul de baza — fara surprize.

content.en: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass **without altering the correctness** of the program. If `S` is a subclass of `T`, then a `T` may be replaced by an `S` everywhere, and code written against `T` must keep working.
content.ro: Obiectele unei superclase ar trebui sa poata fi inlocuite cu obiecte ale unei subclase **fara a altera corectitudinea** programului. Daca `S` este o subclasa a lui `T`, atunci un `T` poate fi inlocuit cu un `S` peste tot, iar codul scris fata de `T` trebuie sa functioneze in continuare.

content.en: Here is a hierarchy that **breaks** LSP. `Bird` declares `fly()` as something every bird can do — but `Penguin` cannot deliver on that promise:
content.ro: Iata o ierarhie care **incalca** LSP. `Bird` declara `fly()` ca ceva ce orice pasare poate face — dar `Penguin` nu se poate tine de aceasta promisiune:

content.en: `Penguin::fly()` is correct C++ — it compiles and runs. But it **violates LSP**: any code that accepts a `Bird` and calls `fly()` silently assumes flight will succeed. A `Penguin` breaks that assumption at runtime. The type system said "yes"; the behaviour said "no".
content.ro: `Penguin::fly()` este C++ corect — compileaza si ruleaza. Dar **incalca LSP**: orice cod care accepta un `Bird` si apeleaza `fly()` presupune tacit ca zborul va reusi. Un `Penguin` strica aceasta presupunere la runtime. Sistemul de tipuri a spus "da"; comportamentul a spus "nu".

content.en: The fix: do not put `fly()` on `Bird`. Split the hierarchy so that only birds that genuinely fly carry the `fly()` contract. `Penguin` stays a `Bird`, but is simply not a `BirdThatCanFly`:
content.ro: Solutia: nu pune `fly()` pe `Bird`. Imparte ierarhia astfel incat doar pasarile care chiar zboara sa poarte contractul `fly()`. `Penguin` ramane un `Bird`, dar pur si simplu nu este un `BirdThatCanFly`:

content.en: **Misconception:** "A penguin **is a** bird in real life, so `Penguin : public Bird` is obviously correct." Inheritance models a **behavioural contract**, not a biology textbook. The question is never "is X a kind of Y in English?" — it is "can an X be used everywhere a Y is expected, with no surprises?"
content.ro: **Conceptie gresita:** "Un pinguin **este o** pasare in viata reala, deci `Penguin : public Bird` este evident corect." Mostenirea modeleaza un **contract comportamental**, nu un manual de biologie. Intrebarea nu este niciodata "este X un fel de Y in romana?" — ci "poate fi folosit un X oriunde este asteptat un Y, fara surprize?"

question.en: The classic LSP puzzle: "a square is a rectangle", so `Square : public Rectangle` looks natural. Yet code that does `r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); assert(r.area() == 20);` breaks if `r` is really a `Square`. Why — and what does this tell you about modelling IS-A relationships?
question.ro: Enigma clasica LSP: "un patrat este un dreptunghi", deci `Square : public Rectangle` pare natural. Totusi, cod care face `r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); assert(r.area() == 20);` se strica daca `r` este de fapt un `Square`. De ce — si ce iti spune asta despre modelarea relatiilor IS-A?

answer.en: A `Square` must keep width and height equal, so `setHeight(4)` also forces width to 4 — `area()` becomes 16, not 20. The base `Rectangle` promised that width and height are **independent**; `Square` cannot honour that promise. The lesson: IS-A in inheritance is about **substitutable behaviour**, not nouns. Geometrically a square is a rectangle, but a **mutable** `Square` is not a behavioural subtype of a **mutable** `Rectangle`. When in doubt, prefer composition or a shared abstraction over forcing an IS-A.
answer.ro: Un `Square` trebuie sa pastreze latimea si inaltimea egale, deci `setHeight(4)` forteaza si latimea la 4 — `area()` devine 16, nu 20. Baza `Rectangle` a promis ca latimea si inaltimea sunt **independente**; `Square` nu poate respecta acea promisiune. Lectia: IS-A in mostenire tine de **comportament substituibil**, nu de substantive. Geometric un patrat este un dreptunghi, dar un `Square` **mutabil** nu este un subtip comportamental al unui `Rectangle` **mutabil**. La indoiala, prefera compozitia sau o abstractizare comuna in locul fortarii unui IS-A.

note.en: Course 12, section "SOLID Principles" — Liskov Substitution Principle.
note.ro: Cursul 12, sectiunea "SOLID Principles" — Principiul Substitutiei Liskov.

question.en: You design one big `Animal` interface with `eat()`, `swim()`, and `fly()`. Now you must write a `Dog` class. The compiler forces `Dog` to implement `fly()` — even though dogs do not fly. What did the fat interface cost you?
question.ro: Proiectezi o singura interfata mare `Animal` cu `eat()`, `swim()` si `fly()`. Acum trebuie sa scrii o clasa `Dog`. Compilatorul forteaza `Dog` sa implementeze `fly()` — desi cainii nu zboara. Ce te-a costat interfata grasa?

answer.en: It forced `Dog` to depend on a method it does not use, and to write a fake or throwing `fly()`. That fake implementation is a lie waiting to be called. The Interface Segregation Principle says: split the fat interface into small ones, so each class implements only what it actually does.
answer.ro: A fortat `Dog` sa depinda de o metoda pe care nu o foloseste si sa scrie un `fly()` fals sau care arunca. Acea implementare falsa este o minciuna care asteapta sa fie apelata. Principiul Segregarii Interfetelor spune: imparte interfata grasa in unele mici, ca fiecare clasa sa implementeze doar ce face cu adevarat.

content.en: Classes should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. An interface (or abstract class) should contain **only the methods relevant** to the classes implementing it. Many small, specific interfaces beat one large, all-purpose interface.
content.ro: Clasele nu ar trebui fortate sa depinda de interfete pe care nu le folosesc. O interfata (sau clasa abstracta) ar trebui sa contina **doar metodele relevante** pentru clasele care o implementeaza. Multe interfete mici si specifice bat o singura interfata mare, universala.

content.en: A single `Animal` interface that declares `eat()`, `swim()`, and `fly()` implies that **every** animal can do all three. That is false for almost every real animal. The interface is too fat — it segregates badly.
content.ro: O singura interfata `Animal` care declara `eat()`, `swim()` si `fly()` implica faptul ca **fiecare** animal le poate face pe toate trei. Acest lucru este fals pentru aproape orice animal real. Interfata este prea grasa — segrega prost.

content.en: The fix: many small interfaces. A class then inherits exactly the capabilities it has — `Dog` eats and swims, `Eagle` eats and flies, and neither is forced to fake anything:
content.ro: Solutia: multe interfete mici. O clasa mosteneste atunci exact capabilitatile pe care le are — `Dog` mananca si inoata, `Eagle` mananca si zboara, si niciuna nu este fortata sa falsifice ceva:

question.en: Before reading on — with one fat `Animal` interface declaring `eat()`, `swim()`, and `fly()`, what is a `Cat` class forced to do about `swim()` and `fly()`, and why is that dangerous?
question.ro: Inainte de a citi mai departe — cu o singura interfata grasa `Animal` care declara `eat()`, `swim()` si `fly()`, ce este o clasa `Cat` fortata sa faca pentru `swim()` si `fly()`, si de ce este periculos?

answer.en: It must provide a body for both — typically a do-nothing stub or one that throws — even though a cat does neither. That fake implementation is a latent bug: any code holding the `Animal` interface may call `fly()` on the cat and get silent wrong behaviour or a crash. ISP removes the dilemma: the cat simply does not implement interfaces for capabilities it lacks.
answer.ro: Trebuie sa ofere un corp pentru amandoua — de obicei un ciot care nu face nimic sau unul care arunca — desi o pisica nu face niciuna. Acea implementare falsa este un bug latent: orice cod care detine interfata `Animal` poate apela `fly()` pe pisica si poate primi comportament gresit tacut sau un crash. ISP elimina dilema: pisica pur si simplu nu implementeaza interfete pentru capabilitati pe care nu le are.

content.en: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules — **both should depend on abstractions**. And abstractions should not depend on details; details should depend on abstractions. In practice: business logic depends on an interface, and concrete implementations are plugged in from outside.
content.ro: Modulele de nivel inalt nu ar trebui sa depinda de modulele de nivel scazut — **amandoua ar trebui sa depinda de abstractizari**. Iar abstractizarile nu ar trebui sa depinda de detalii; detaliile ar trebui sa depinda de abstractizari. In practica: logica de business depinde de o interfata, iar implementarile concrete sunt conectate din exterior.

content.en: In the example below, `Computer` is the high-level module. It does **not** depend on `Keyboard` or `Mouse` directly — it depends on the `Input` abstraction. `Keyboard` and `Mouse` (the low-level details) also depend on `Input`. The dependency has been **inverted**: instead of high-level pointing at low-level, both point at the abstraction. This is what gives **low coupling**:
content.ro: In exemplul de mai jos, `Computer` este modulul de nivel inalt. El **nu** depinde direct de `Keyboard` sau `Mouse` — depinde de abstractizarea `Input`. `Keyboard` si `Mouse` (detaliile de nivel scazut) depind si ele de `Input`. Dependenta a fost **inversata**: in loc ca nivelul inalt sa arate spre nivelul scazut, amandoua arata spre abstractizare. Asta da **cuplaj scazut**:

question.en: You want to unit-test `Computer::process_input()` without a real keyboard or mouse. How do ISP and DIP together make that trivial — and what would you have to do instead if `Computer` had hard-coded a concrete `Keyboard` member?
question.ro: Vrei sa testezi unitar `Computer::process_input()` fara o tastatura sau un mouse real. Cum fac ISP si DIP impreuna ca acest lucru sa fie trivial — si ce ar trebui sa faci in schimb daca `Computer` ar fi avut hardcodat un membru `Keyboard` concret?

answer.en: Because `Computer` depends only on the small `Input` abstraction (ISP keeps it small; DIP makes `Computer` depend on it), you can write a `FakeInput : public Input` that returns a scripted string and pass it to the constructor. The test needs no hardware. If `Computer` had a concrete `Keyboard` member, you could not substitute it — you would be forced to either run real hardware, or edit `Computer` itself for testing (breaking OCP). DIP is what makes code **testable by construction**: every external dependency enters through an interface you can replace.
answer.ro: Pentru ca `Computer` depinde doar de abstractizarea mica `Input` (ISP o tine mica; DIP face `Computer` sa depinda de ea), poti scrie un `FakeInput : public Input` care returneaza un sir prestabilit si il trimiti constructorului. Testul nu are nevoie de hardware. Daca `Computer` ar fi avut un membru `Keyboard` concret, nu l-ai putea inlocui — ai fi fortat fie sa rulezi hardware real, fie sa modifici `Computer` insusi pentru testare (incalcand OCP). DIP este ce face codul **testabil prin constructie**: fiecare dependenta externa intra printr-o interfata pe care o poti inlocui.

note.en: Course 12, section "SOLID Principles" — Interface Segregation & Dependency Inversion. DIP promotes low coupling between modules.
note.ro: Cursul 12, sectiunea "SOLID Principles" — Segregarea Interfetelor si Inversiunea Dependentelor. DIP promoveaza cuplajul scazut intre module.

title.ro: Gang of Four si Categoriile de Sabloane

question.en: SOLID gave you principles — general advice. But experienced developers noticed something stronger: the **same design problems** recur across unrelated projects, and so do the **same solutions**. What would it be worth to give each of those recurring solutions a name and a documented structure?
question.ro: SOLID ti-a dat principii — sfaturi generale. Dar dezvoltatorii experimentati au observat ceva mai puternic: **aceleasi probleme de proiectare** reapar in proiecte fara legatura, si la fel si **aceleasi solutii**. Ce ar merita sa dai fiecareia dintre aceste solutii recurente un nume si o structura documentata?

answer.en: You would get a shared **vocabulary**: instead of describing ten lines of design, you say one word — "use a Factory here" — and everyone understands. That catalogue of named solutions is exactly what design patterns are, and the Gang of Four wrote the book on them.
answer.ro: Ai obtine un **vocabular** comun: in loc sa descrii zece linii de proiectare, spui un singur cuvant — "foloseste un Factory aici" — si toata lumea intelege. Acel catalog de solutii numite este exact ce sunt design pattern-urile, iar Gang of Four a scris cartea despre ele.

content.en: **GoF** stands for **Gang of Four** — the nickname for the four authors of the influential 1994 software engineering book **Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software**.
content.ro: **GoF** inseamna **Gang of Four** (Banda celor Patru) — porecla celor patru autori ai influentei carti de inginerie software din 1994, **Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software**.

content.en: A general, reusable solution to a problem that occurs commonly in software design. It is **not finished code** — it is a template or best practice you adapt to your specific context. A pattern has a name, a problem description, a solution structure, and known consequences.
content.ro: O solutie generala si reutilizabila pentru o problema care apare frecvent in proiectarea software. Nu este **cod terminat** — este un sablon sau o buna practica pe care o adaptezi contextului tau specific. Un pattern are un nume, o descriere a problemei, o structura de solutie si consecinte cunoscute.

items.en: **Language-independent** — patterns describe concepts, not syntax. The same Observer works in C++, Java, or Python.
items.ro: **Independente de limbaj** — pattern-urile descriu concepte, nu sintaxa. Acelasi Observer functioneaza in C++, Java sau Python.

items.en: **Reusable** — once learned, a pattern applies across many projects.
items.ro: **Reutilizabile** — odata invatat, un pattern se aplica in multe proiecte.

items.en: **Proven** — patterns are time-tested solutions used by experienced developers.
items.ro: **Verificate** — pattern-urile sunt solutii testate de timp, folosite de dezvoltatori experimentati.

items.en: **Documented structure** — each pattern has a name, problem, solution, and consequences.
items.ro: **Structura documentata** — fiecare pattern are un nume, o problema, o solutie si consecinte.

content.en: A pattern is **not** a code snippet to paste. It is a description of how classes and objects relate to solve a recurring problem. Copy-pasting a Singleton without understanding **why** it fits your problem is how patterns get misused.
content.ro: Un pattern **nu** este un fragment de cod de lipit. Este o descriere a modului in care clasele si obiectele se relationeaza pentru a rezolva o problema recurenta. Copierea unui Singleton fara a intelege **de ce** se potriveste problemei tale este modul in care pattern-urile sunt folosite gresit.

question.en: Why is a shared pattern vocabulary worth more on a **team** than for a solo developer working alone?
question.ro: De ce valoreaza un vocabular comun de pattern-uri mai mult intr-o **echipa** decat pentru un dezvoltator singur care lucreaza de unul singur?

answer.en: Communication. On a team, design intent must cross between people — in code review, in a design doc, at a whiteboard. "This class is a Visitor over the AST" instantly conveys structure, intent, and trade-offs to anyone who knows the pattern; the alternative is a paragraph of prose that each reader interprets slightly differently. Patterns compress design discussion into a few precise nouns. A solo developer still benefits (patterns are proven solutions), but the **communication** multiplier only appears once more than one mind must share the same mental model.
answer.ro: Comunicarea. Intr-o echipa, intentia de proiectare trebuie sa treaca intre oameni — la code review, intr-un document de design, la tabla. "Aceasta clasa este un Visitor peste AST" transmite instant structura, intentia si compromisurile oricui cunoaste pattern-ul; alternativa este un paragraf de proza pe care fiecare cititor il interpreteaza usor diferit. Pattern-urile comprima discutia de design in cateva substantive precise. Un dezvoltator singur tot beneficiaza (pattern-urile sunt solutii verificate), dar multiplicatorul de **comunicare** apare doar cand mai mult de o minte trebuie sa imparta acelasi model mental.

note.ro: Cursul 12, sectiunea "Gang of Four (GoF)". Restul cursului parcurge cate un pattern din fiecare categorie.

question.en: Your application needs exactly **one** configuration object — one place that holds settings, shared by the whole program. A plain class does not stop anyone from writing `new Config()` ten times. How do you make "only one instance" a guarantee enforced by the class itself?
question.ro: Aplicatia ta are nevoie de exact **un singur** obiect de configurare — un singur loc care tine setarile, partajat de tot programul. O clasa obisnuita nu impiedica pe nimeni sa scrie `new Config()` de zece ori. Cum faci ca "o singura instanta" sa fie o garantie impusa de clasa insasi?

answer.en: Make the constructor **private** so no outside code can call `new`, and expose a **static** function that creates the instance once and returns the same one every time afterwards. That combination is the Singleton pattern.
answer.ro: Fa constructorul **privat** ca niciun cod din afara sa nu poata apela `new`, si expune o functie **statica** care creeaza instanta o singura data si returneaza aceeasi instanta de fiecare data dupa aceea. Aceasta combinatie este pattern-ul Singleton.

content.en: A creational pattern that restricts a class to **a single instance** and provides one global access point to it. Built from two pieces: a private constructor (blocks external `new`) and a static accessor (creates the instance lazily, then hands out the same one).
content.ro: Un pattern creational care restrange o clasa la **o singura instanta** si ofera un singur punct global de acces la ea. Construit din doua piese: un constructor privat (blocheaza `new`-ul extern) si un accesor static (creeaza instanta lenes, apoi distribuie mereu aceeasi).

content.en:
**Three things people get wrong about Singleton:**
1. **It is just a global variable.** No — a global gives no control over **when** it is created and no way to block extra instances. Singleton enforces both.
2. **This lazy init is thread-safe.** It is **not** — two threads can both see `instance == nullptr` and both call `new`. Real code needs a mutex or a `static` local (C++11 guarantees that one).
3. **Singleton is always good design.** It is a hidden global and makes testing harder. Use it sparingly.
content.ro:
**Trei lucruri pe care lumea le intelege gresit despre Singleton:**
1. **Este doar o variabila globala.** Nu — o globala nu da control asupra momentului **cand** este creata si nicio cale de a bloca instante suplimentare. Singleton le impune pe amandoua.
2. **Aceasta initializare lenesa este thread-safe.** **Nu este** — doua fire pot vedea amandoua `instance == nullptr` si pot apela amandoua `new`. Codul real are nevoie de un mutex sau de o variabila locala `static` (C++11 o garanteaza pe aceea).
3. **Singleton este mereu un design bun.** Este o globala ascunsa si ingreuneaza testarea. Foloseste-l cu masura.

content.en: **Variant 1 — a bounded number of instances.** The Singleton idea generalises: instead of exactly one, allow at most `MAX_INSTANCES`. A static array holds the instances and a static counter caps creation:
content.ro: **Varianta 1 — un numar limitat de instante.** Ideea de Singleton se generalizeaza: in loc de exact una, permite cel mult `MAX_INSTANCES`. Un tablou static tine instantele iar un contor static limiteaza crearea:

content.en: **Variant 2 — a generic, reusable Singleton.** Writing the private-constructor + static-accessor boilerplate for every class is tedious. A class **template** captures it once; any type becomes a singleton by inheriting from `Singleton<T>`:
content.ro: **Varianta 2 — un Singleton generic, reutilizabil.** Scrierea sablonului constructor-privat + accesor-static pentru fiecare clasa este obositoare. Un **template** de clasa il capteaza o singura data; orice tip devine un singleton mostenind din `Singleton<T>`:

content.en: A creational pattern that **extends Singleton** by allowing controlled access to **multiple instances, each identified by a unique key**. Where Singleton answers "give me **the** instance", Multiton answers "give me the instance **for this key**" — creating it on first request and reusing it afterwards.
content.ro: Un pattern creational care **extinde Singleton** permitand acces controlat la **mai multe instante, fiecare identificata printr-o cheie unica**. Acolo unde Singleton raspunde la "da-mi **acea** instanta", Multiton raspunde la "da-mi instanta **pentru aceasta cheie**" — creand-o la prima cerere si reutilizand-o dupa aceea.

items.en: Multi-lingual support — one `Translator` instance per language.
items.ro: Suport multi-lingvistic — o instanta `Translator` per limba.

items.en: Named resources — one cached object per resource name.
items.ro: Resurse cu nume — un obiect din cache per nume de resursa.

items.en: Configuration set by the environment — one config per profile.
items.ro: Configurare setata de mediu — o configurare per profil.

question.en: A Multiton is basically `GetInstance(key)` over a `map<key, Object>`. So why call it a pattern at all — what does the `GetInstance` wrapper give you that a plain public `std::unordered_map<std::string, Object>` does not?
question.ro: Un Multiton este in esenta `GetInstance(key)` peste un `map<key, Object>`. Atunci de ce sa-l numim pattern — ce iti ofera invelisul `GetInstance` pe care un `std::unordered_map<std::string, Object>` public obisnuit nu il ofera?

answer.en: Control over creation and uniqueness. With a plain public map, any code can insert, overwrite, or create a second object for the same key — and the constructor is public, so the "one per key" rule is just a convention nobody enforces. The `GetInstance` wrapper, paired with a **private constructor**, makes the rule structural: there is exactly one code path that creates an `Object`, it checks the map first, and callers physically cannot bypass it. The pattern is not the map — it is the **enforced invariant** that the map enables.
answer.ro: Controlul asupra crearii si unicitatii. Cu un map public obisnuit, orice cod poate insera, suprascrie sau crea un al doilea obiect pentru aceeasi cheie — iar constructorul este public, deci regula "unul per cheie" este doar o conventie pe care nimeni nu o impune. Invelisul `GetInstance`, impreuna cu un **constructor privat**, face regula structurala: exista exact o singura cale de cod care creeaza un `Object`, ea verifica map-ul mai intai, iar apelantii nu pot fizic sa o ocoleasca. Pattern-ul nu este map-ul — este **invariantul impus** pe care map-ul il face posibil.

note.ro: Cursul 12, sectiunile "Singleton" si "Multiton" — pattern-urile creationale. Variantele MAX_INSTANCES si template sunt extensii adaugate de Prof. Gavrilut.

question.en: Your client code is full of `if (type == "dog") a = new Dog(); else if (type == "cat") a = new Cat();` — and that same chain is copy-pasted in five files. Adding a `Hamster` means hunting down all five. What would centralise this?
question.ro: Codul tau client este plin de `if (type == "dog") a = new Dog(); else if (type == "cat") a = new Cat();` — iar acel lant este copiat in cinci fisiere. Adaugarea unui `Hamster` inseamna sa vanezi toate cinci. Ce ar centraliza asta?

answer.en: Move the type-decision into a single place — a Factory. Client code asks the factory for an object by description; only the factory knows the concrete classes. Adding `Hamster` means editing one function.
answer.ro: Muta decizia de tip intr-un singur loc — un Factory. Codul client cere fabricii un obiect dupa descriere; doar fabrica stie clasele concrete. Adaugarea lui `Hamster` inseamna modificarea unei singure functii.

content.en: A creational pattern that defines an interface for creating an object but lets a method or class decide which concrete class to instantiate. Instead of calling `new` directly, client code calls a **factory**, which encapsulates the choice of concrete type.
content.ro: Un pattern creational care defineste o interfata pentru crearea unui obiect dar lasa o metoda sau o clasa sa decida ce clasa concreta sa instantieze. In loc sa apeleze `new` direct, codul client apeleaza o **fabrica**, care incapsuleaza alegerea tipului concret.

content.en: The Factory is where the `new` calls are concentrated. The rest of the program depends only on the `Animal` abstraction — which is exactly the Dependency Inversion Principle in action. Adding a new animal type touches one function instead of five files.
content.ro: Fabrica este locul unde sunt concentrate apelurile `new`. Restul programului depinde doar de abstractizarea `Animal` — ceea ce este exact Principiul Inversiunii Dependentelor in actiune. Adaugarea unui tip nou de animal atinge o singura functie in loc de cinci fisiere.

content.en: A creational pattern that separates the **construction** of a complex object from its **representation**, so the same construction process can produce different results. The object is assembled step by step rather than through one giant constructor.
content.ro: Un pattern creational care separa **constructia** unui obiect complex de **reprezentarea** lui, astfel incat acelasi proces de constructie sa poata produce rezultate diferite. Obiectul este asamblat pas cu pas in loc de un singur constructor gigant.

blocks.code:
// Each Set... returns *this, so the calls chain (a "fluent interface").
// build() produces the finished, fully-configured object.
auto c = CarBuilder()
             .SetColor("Red")
             .SetFuel(300)
             .SetHorsePower(150)
             .SetManualSteering(true)
             .SetSpeed(120)
             .SetTireType("Summer")
             .SetName("Audi")
             .build();

content.en: Builder shines when an object has **many optional parameters**. The alternative — one constructor with eight arguments — is the **telescoping constructor** problem: `Car("Red", 300, 150, true, 120, "Summer", "Audi")` is unreadable and easy to get wrong by argument order. The named `Set...` calls are self-documenting and order-independent.
content.ro: Builder straluceste cand un obiect are **multi parametri optionali**. Alternativa — un constructor cu opt argumente — este problema **constructorului telescopic**: `Car("Red", 300, 150, true, 120, "Summer", "Audi")` este ilizibil si usor de gresit prin ordinea argumentelor. Apelurile `Set...` cu nume se auto-documenteaza si nu depind de ordine.

question.en: Both Factory and Builder are creational patterns that avoid raw `new` in client code. In one sentence each: when do you reach for a Factory, and when for a Builder?
question.ro: Atat Factory cat si Builder sunt pattern-uri creationale care evita `new`-ul brut in codul client. Intr-o propozitie fiecare: cand alegi un Factory si cand un Builder?

answer.en: Reach for a **Factory** when the hard part is **choosing which class** to instantiate from several options (the result type varies, construction is simple). Reach for a **Builder** when the class is fixed but **assembling one instance is complex** — many optional fields, a multi-step process, or several valid representations. Factory = "which type?"; Builder = "how to assemble this one?".
answer.ro: Alege un **Factory** cand partea grea este **alegerea clasei** de instantiat dintre mai multe optiuni (tipul rezultatului variaza, constructia este simpla). Alege un **Builder** cand clasa este fixa dar **asamblarea unei instante este complexa** — multe campuri optionale, un proces in mai multi pasi sau mai multe reprezentari valide. Factory = "ce tip?"; Builder = "cum asamblez aceasta instanta?".

note.en: Course 12, sections "Factory" and "Builder" — the remaining creational patterns.
note.ro: Cursul 12, sectiunile "Factory" si "Builder" — pattern-urile creationale ramase.

question.en: You have a `Bicycle` class with a `move()` method. A large part of your codebase is written against a `Car` interface and calls `drive()`. You cannot change `Bicycle` (third-party) and you cannot change all the call sites. How do you let a `Bicycle` be used where a `Car` is expected?
question.ro: Ai o clasa `Bicycle` cu o metoda `move()`. O mare parte din codul tau este scrisa fata de o interfata `Car` si apeleaza `drive()`. Nu poti schimba `Bicycle` (terta parte) si nu poti schimba toate locurile de apel. Cum lasi un `Bicycle` sa fie folosit acolo unde este asteptat un `Car`?

answer.en: Write a thin class that **is-a** `Car` (so it fits the expected interface), holds a `Bicycle` inside, and translates each `Car` call into the matching `Bicycle` call. That translator is the Adapter pattern.
answer.ro: Scrie o clasa subtire care **este-un** `Car` (ca sa se incadreze in interfata asteptata), tine un `Bicycle` in interior si traduce fiecare apel `Car` in apelul `Bicycle` corespunzator. Acel traducator este pattern-ul Adapter.

content.en: A structural pattern that converts the interface of a class into another interface that clients expect. Adapter lets classes work together that otherwise could not, because their interfaces are incompatible.
content.ro: Un pattern structural care converteste interfata unei clase intr-o alta interfata pe care clientii o asteapta. Adapter lasa clase care altfel nu ar putea, sa lucreze impreuna, deoarece interfetele lor sunt incompatibile.

content.en: A structural pattern that composes objects into **tree structures** to represent part-whole hierarchies. Composite lets clients treat **individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly** — the same call works on a leaf and on a whole subtree.
content.ro: Un pattern structural care compune obiecte in **structuri de arbore** pentru a reprezenta ierarhii parte-intreg. Composite lasa clientii sa trateze **obiectele individuale si compozitiile de obiecte uniform** — acelasi apel functioneaza pe o frunza si pe un intreg subarbore.

content.en: A UI is the classic Composite. A desktop contains windows; a window contains panels; a panel contains buttons. A button is a leaf; the rest are composites. Yet the client just calls `Paint()` on the root:
content.ro: O interfata grafica este Composite-ul clasic. Un desktop contine ferestre; o fereastra contine panouri; un panou contine butoane. Un buton este o frunza; restul sunt composite. Totusi clientul doar apeleaza `Paint()` pe radacina:

blocks.code:
Desktop Object
  |
  +-- Window Object
        |
        +-- Panel Object
              |
              +-- A Button   (leaf -- no children)

content.en: The power of Composite: the client calls `Paint()` on the `Desktop` and the **whole tree** paints itself — each composite forwards the call to its children, each leaf just paints. No `if (isContainer) ... else ...` branching anywhere. Leaf and container expose the **same** `Widget` interface.
content.ro: Puterea lui Composite: clientul apeleaza `Paint()` pe `Desktop` si **tot arborele** se deseneaza singur — fiecare composite trimite apelul mai departe copiilor sai, fiecare frunza doar se deseneaza. Nicio ramificare `if (isContainer) ... else ...` nicaieri. Frunza si containerul expun **aceeasi** interfata `Widget`.

question.en: Adapter and Composite are both "structural" patterns. What does "structural" mean here, and how do the two differ in **intent** — what problem is each one actually solving?
question.ro: Adapter si Composite sunt amandoua pattern-uri "structurale". Ce inseamna "structural" aici, si cum difera cele doua ca **intentie** — ce problema rezolva de fapt fiecare?

answer.en: "Structural" means the pattern is about **how classes and objects are composed** into larger structures — the wiring, not the creation (creational) or the messaging (behavioral). Within that: **Adapter** is about **compatibility** — making one existing interface usable where a different one is expected, without changing either side. **Composite** is about **uniformity at scale** — letting a tree of objects be treated exactly like a single object, so client code never special-cases "one" versus "many". Adapter bridges two shapes; Composite makes a whole hierarchy present one shape.
answer.ro: "Structural" inseamna ca pattern-ul tine de **cum sunt compuse clasele si obiectele** in structuri mai mari — conectarea, nu crearea (creational) sau mesageria (comportamental). In cadrul asta: **Adapter** tine de **compatibilitate** — a face o interfata existenta utilizabila acolo unde este asteptata alta, fara a schimba vreo parte. **Composite** tine de **uniformitate la scara** — a lasa un arbore de obiecte sa fie tratat exact ca un singur obiect, astfel incat codul client sa nu trateze niciodata separat "unul" fata de "mai multe". Adapter face puntea intre doua forme; Composite face ca o intreaga ierarhie sa prezinte o singura forma.

note.ro: Cursul 12, sectiunile "Adapter" si "Composite" — pattern-urile structurale. Arborele desktop/fereastra/panou/buton este diagrama de la pagina 94 a cursului.

question.en: You have a stable hierarchy — `Dog`, `Cat`, `Bird` — and they will not change. But you keep needing **new operations** over them: make a sound, compute a vet bill, export to JSON, draw an icon. Adding each operation as a method to every class bloats all of them and mixes unrelated concerns. What is the alternative?
question.ro: Ai o ierarhie stabila — `Dog`, `Cat`, `Bird` — si nu se va schimba. Dar tot ai nevoie de **operatii noi** peste ele: scoate un sunet, calculeaza nota de plata la veterinar, exporta in JSON, deseneaza o iconita. Adaugarea fiecarei operatii ca metoda in fiecare clasa le umfla pe toate si amesteca preocupari fara legatura. Care este alternativa?

answer.en: Pull each operation out into its own object — a Visitor. The element classes stay untouched; a new operation is a new visitor class. The Visitor pattern lets you add operations without editing the elements.
answer.ro: Extrage fiecare operatie in propriul obiect — un Visitor. Clasele element raman neatinse; o operatie noua este o clasa visitor noua. Pattern-ul Visitor iti permite sa adaugi operatii fara sa modifici elementele.

content.en: A behavioral pattern that represents an **operation to be performed on the elements of an object structure**. Visitor lets you define a new operation without changing the classes of the elements it operates on.
content.ro: Un pattern comportamental care reprezinta o **operatie de efectuat pe elementele unei structuri de obiecte**. Visitor iti permite sa definesti o operatie noua fara a schimba clasele elementelor pe care opereaza.

content.en: The piece that wires it together is the `accept()` method on each element. The element calls `visitor.visit(*this)` — and because `*this` has a known concrete type **inside** `Dog`, the right `visit()` overload is chosen. This two-step resolution is called **double dispatch**:
content.ro: Piesa care leaga totul este metoda `accept()` de pe fiecare element. Elementul apeleaza `visitor.visit(*this)` — si pentru ca `*this` are un tip concret cunoscut **in interiorul** lui `Dog`, este aleasa supraincarcarea `visit()` corecta. Aceasta rezolvare in doi pasi se numeste **double dispatch**:

content.en: **The Visitor trade-off — know it before you use it.** Visitor makes adding a new **operation** cheap (one new visitor class) but adding a new **element type** expensive: a new `Fish` forces a `visit(Fish&)` into the `Visitor` base **and into every existing concrete visitor**. Choose Visitor only when the element hierarchy is stable and the operations keep growing — not the other way around.
content.ro: **Compromisul Visitor — afla-l inainte sa-l folosesti.** Visitor face adaugarea unei **operatii** noi ieftina (o clasa visitor noua) dar adaugarea unui **tip de element** nou scumpa: un `Fish` nou forteaza un `visit(Fish&)` in baza `Visitor` **si in fiecare visitor concret existent**. Alege Visitor doar cand ierarhia de elemente este stabila iar operatiile tot cresc — nu invers.

question.en: Visitor lets you add operations without touching the element classes — that sounds like the Open-Closed Principle. Yet the trap above says adding a new element type forces edits to every visitor. So does Visitor obey OCP or violate it?
question.ro: Visitor iti permite sa adaugi operatii fara sa atingi clasele element — asta suna a Principiul Deschis-Inchis. Totusi capcana de mai sus spune ca adaugarea unui tip de element nou forteaza modificari in fiecare visitor. Deci Visitor respecta OCP sau il incalca?

answer.en: Both — it depends on the axis. OCP is always relative to **what kind of change** you expect. Along the **operations** axis, Visitor is perfectly open-closed: a new operation is a new class, zero edits to elements. Along the **element-types** axis, Visitor is the opposite: a new element is a breaking change to every visitor. Visitor does not abolish the cost of change; it **relocates** it onto the axis you declared stable. The design skill is predicting correctly which axis will actually move — if elements churn and operations are fixed, Visitor is the wrong pattern.
answer.ro: Amandoua — depinde de axa. OCP este mereu relativ la **ce fel de schimbare** astepti. Pe axa **operatiilor**, Visitor este perfect deschis-inchis: o operatie noua este o clasa noua, zero modificari in elemente. Pe axa **tipurilor de element**, Visitor este opusul: un element nou este o schimbare cu rupere in fiecare visitor. Visitor nu desfiinteaza costul schimbarii; il **muta** pe axa pe care ai declarat-o stabila. Abilitatea de proiectare este sa prezici corect care axa se va misca de fapt — daca elementele se schimba des si operatiile sunt fixe, Visitor este pattern-ul gresit.

content.en: **Exam relevance:** the Visitor pattern has appeared as a dedicated implementation problem in past UAIC OOP exams (2023-2024 second-test problem set). Be ready to write the `accept()` / `visit()` wiring by hand, not just recognise it.
content.ro: **Relevanta pentru examen:** pattern-ul Visitor a aparut ca problema de implementare dedicata in examene OOP UAIC anterioare (setul de probleme de la testul 2, 2023-2024). Fii pregatit sa scrii conectarea `accept()` / `visit()` de mana, nu doar sa o recunosti.

note.ro: Cursul 12, sectiunea "Visitor" — un pattern comportamental. Conectarea double-dispatch accept()/visit() completeaza schita Visitor/SoundVisitor a profesorului.

question.en: A YouTube channel uploads a video. Ten thousand subscribers must each be notified. The channel must not hard-code who the subscribers are — they sign up and leave at runtime. How do you let the channel announce "new video" without knowing anything about the individual subscribers?
question.ro: Un canal de YouTube incarca un video. Zece mii de abonati trebuie notificati fiecare. Canalul nu trebuie sa hardcodeze cine sunt abonatii — ei se inscriu si pleaca la runtime. Cum lasi canalul sa anunte "video nou" fara sa stie nimic despre abonatii individuali?

answer.en: Let subscribers register themselves with the channel through a common `Observer` interface. The channel keeps a list of `Observer*` and, on a new upload, calls `notify()` on each. The channel knows only the interface — never the concrete subscribers. That is the Observer pattern.
answer.ro: Lasa abonatii sa se inregistreze singuri la canal printr-o interfata `Observer` comuna. Canalul tine o lista de `Observer*` si, la o incarcare noua, apeleaza `notify()` pe fiecare. Canalul cunoaste doar interfata — niciodata abonatii concreti. Acesta este pattern-ul Observer.

content.en: A behavioral pattern that defines a **one-to-many dependency** between objects: when one object (the subject) changes state, all its dependents (the observers) are notified and updated automatically.
content.ro: Un pattern comportamental care defineste o **dependenta unu-la-multi** intre obiecte: cand un obiect (subiectul) isi schimba starea, toti dependentii lui (observatorii) sunt notificati si actualizati automat.

content.en: Observer decouples the subject from its observers. `YouTubeChannel` depends only on the `Observer` interface — it can notify a phone app, an email service, and a logger without a single line that mentions any of them. New observer types plug in with no change to the channel (Open-Closed Principle again).
content.ro: Observer decupleaza subiectul de observatorii sai. `YouTubeChannel` depinde doar de interfata `Observer` — poate notifica o aplicatie de telefon, un serviciu de email si un logger fara o singura linie care sa mentioneze vreunul dintre ele. Tipuri noi de observator se conecteaza fara nicio schimbare in canal (din nou Principiul Deschis-Inchis).

content.en: A behavioral pattern that avoids coupling the sender of a request to its receiver by giving **more than one object a chance to handle it**. The receivers are chained; the request travels along the chain until an object handles it.
content.ro: Un pattern comportamental care evita cuplarea expeditorului unei cereri de receptorul ei, oferind **mai multor obiecte sansa de a o trata**. Receptorii sunt inlantuiti; cererea calatoreste de-a lungul lantului pana cand un obiect o trateaza.

content.en: Chain of Responsibility maps naturally onto the Composite tree from the previous step. A key press lands on a `Button`; if the button does not handle it, `SendKeyToParent` passes it to the `Panel`, then the `Window`, then the `Desktop`. The sender (the key event) never needs to know which level will deal with it.
content.ro: Chain of Responsibility se mapeaza natural pe arborele Composite din pasul anterior. O apasare de tasta ajunge pe un `Button`; daca butonul nu o trateaza, `SendKeyToParent` o trimite la `Panel`, apoi la `Window`, apoi la `Desktop`. Expeditorul (evenimentul de tasta) nu trebuie sa stie niciodata ce nivel se va ocupa de ea.

question.en: Observer and Chain of Responsibility both decouple a sender from its receivers. But the **delivery** differs sharply. Contrast how a message travels in each — and what that implies about how many receivers act on it.
question.ro: Observer si Chain of Responsibility decupleaza amandoua un expeditor de receptorii sai. Dar **livrarea** difera puternic. Contrasteaza cum calatoreste un mesaj in fiecare — si ce implica asta despre cati receptori actioneaza asupra lui.

answer.en: Observer is a **broadcast**: one state change is pushed to **every** registered observer, and all of them react. The relationship is one-to-many and parallel in intent — there is no notion of "someone already handled it". Chain of Responsibility is a **relay**: the request is passed to one candidate at a time, and normally the **first** one able to handle it consumes it and the journey stops. Observer answers "notify everyone interested"; Chain answers "find the one right handler". The first fans out; the second narrows down.
answer.ro: Observer este un **broadcast**: o schimbare de stare este impinsa catre **fiecare** observator inregistrat, si toti reactioneaza. Relatia este unu-la-multi si paralela ca intentie — nu exista notiunea de "cineva deja a tratat-o". Chain of Responsibility este o **stafeta**: cererea este pasata catre un candidat pe rand, iar in mod normal **primul** capabil sa o trateze o consuma si calatoria se opreste. Observer raspunde la "notifica pe toti cei interesati"; Chain raspunde la "gaseste singurul handler potrivit". Primul se ramifica in afara; al doilea ingusteaza.

note.en: Course 12, sections "Observer" and "Chain of Responsibility" — the remaining behavioral patterns and the end of the lecture.
note.ro: Cursul 12, sectiunile "Observer" si "Chain of Responsibility" — pattern-urile comportamentale ramase si finalul cursului.

question.en: A `Report` class can build a report, save it to a database, and email it. According to SRP, what is the problem?
question.ro: O clasa `Report` poate construi un raport, il poate salva intr-o baza de date si il poate trimite pe email. Conform SRP, care este problema?

text.en: Nothing — a class with three methods is small enough to be fine.
text.ro: Nimic — o clasa cu trei metode este suficient de mica ca sa fie in regula.

explanation.en: SRP is not about method count. A class with twenty cohesive getters has one responsibility; this class has three unrelated ones.
explanation.ro: SRP nu tine de numarul de metode. O clasa cu douazeci de getteri coezivi are o responsabilitate; aceasta clasa are trei fara legatura.

text.en: It has three reasons to change — report logic, storage, and email — so a change in any one risks breaking the others.
text.ro: Are trei motive sa se schimbe — logica raportului, stocarea si email-ul — deci o schimbare in oricare risca sa le strice pe celelalte.

explanation.en: Correct. SRP counts reasons to change. Database schema, email API, and report format evolve independently; binding them into one class couples three unrelated concerns.
explanation.ro: Corect. SRP numara motivele de schimbare. Schema bazei de date, API-ul de email si formatul raportului evolueaza independent; legarea lor intr-o clasa cupleaza trei preocupari fara legatura.

text.en: It violates OCP, because adding a fourth method modifies the class.
text.ro: Incalca OCP, deoarece adaugarea unei a patra metode modifica clasa.

explanation.en: The principle in play is SRP (too many responsibilities). OCP is about extending behaviour for new variants without editing tested code — a different concern.
explanation.ro: Principiul implicat este SRP (prea multe responsabilitati). OCP tine de extinderea comportamentului pentru variante noi fara a modifica cod testat — o alta preocupare.

text.en: The class should be a Singleton so only one report exists.
text.ro: Clasa ar trebui sa fie un Singleton ca sa existe un singur raport.

explanation.en: Instance count is unrelated to the problem. The fix is to split the three responsibilities into separate classes.
explanation.ro: Numarul de instante nu are legatura cu problema. Solutia este sa imparti cele trei responsabilitati in clase separate.

question.en: Which design satisfies the Open-Closed Principle for a set of shapes whose `area()` must be computed?
question.ro: Ce design satisface Principiul Deschis-Inchis pentru un set de forme al caror `area()` trebuie calculat?

text.en: One `Shape` class storing a type enum, with `area()` switching on the enum.
text.ro: O clasa `Shape` care stocheaza un enum de tip, cu `area()` care face switch pe enum.

explanation.en: This is the OCP violation: every new shape forces an edit to the enum and the switch inside already-tested code.
explanation.ro: Aceasta este incalcarea OCP: fiecare forma noua forteaza o modificare a enum-ului si a switch-ului in cod deja testat.

text.en: A free function `area(Shape&)` with an `if`/`else` chain over `typeid`.
text.ro: O functie libera `area(Shape&)` cu un lant `if`/`else` peste `typeid`.

explanation.en: Same problem in another shape: each new type means editing the if/else chain. Polymorphic dispatch avoids that entirely.
explanation.ro: Aceeasi problema sub alta forma: fiecare tip nou inseamna modificarea lantului if/else. Dispatch-ul polimorfic evita asta complet.

text.en: Make `Shape` a Singleton and recompute `area()` on each access.
text.ro: Fa din `Shape` un Singleton si recalculeaza `area()` la fiecare acces.

explanation.en: Singleton controls instance count; it has nothing to do with extending a set of shape types without modification.
explanation.ro: Singleton controleaza numarul de instante; nu are nimic de-a face cu extinderea unui set de tipuri de forme fara modificare.

text.en: An abstract `Shape` with a pure virtual `area()`, and one derived class per concrete shape.
text.ro: Un `Shape` abstract cu un `area()` pur virtual, si o clasa derivata per forma concreta.

explanation.en: Correct. A new shape is a new class; the base and existing shapes are never edited. Open for extension, closed for modification.
explanation.ro: Corect. O forma noua este o clasa noua; baza si formele existente nu sunt niciodata modificate. Deschis pentru extindere, inchis pentru modificare.

question.en: `Penguin` inherits from `Bird`, which declares `virtual void fly()`. `Penguin::fly()` throws an exception. Why does this violate the Liskov Substitution Principle?
question.ro: `Penguin` mosteneste din `Bird`, care declara `virtual void fly()`. `Penguin::fly()` arunca o exceptie. De ce incalca asta Principiul Substitutiei Liskov?

text.en: Code written for a `Bird` assumes `fly()` succeeds; substituting a `Penguin` breaks that code at runtime.
text.ro: Codul scris pentru un `Bird` presupune ca `fly()` reuseste; inlocuirea cu un `Penguin` strica acel cod la runtime.

explanation.en: Correct. LSP requires a subtype to be usable everywhere the base is expected, with no surprises. A throwing `fly()` is a surprise that breaks the base's contract.
explanation.ro: Corect. LSP cere ca un subtip sa fie utilizabil oriunde este asteptata baza, fara surprize. Un `fly()` care arunca este o surpriza care strica contractul bazei.

text.en: `Penguin::fly()` does not compile, so the hierarchy is invalid.
text.ro: `Penguin::fly()` nu compileaza, deci ierarhia este invalida.

explanation.en: It compiles fine — throwing is valid C++. The violation is behavioral, not a compile error. That is exactly what makes it dangerous.
explanation.ro: Compileaza fara probleme — a arunca este C++ valid. Incalcarea este comportamentala, nu o eroare de compilare. Exact asta o face periculoasa.

text.en: A penguin is not a bird, so the inheritance is biologically wrong.
text.ro: Un pinguin nu este o pasare, deci mostenirea este gresita biologic.

explanation.en: Biology is not the test. LSP is about substitutable behaviour: the issue is the broken `fly()` contract, not taxonomy.
explanation.ro: Biologia nu este testul. LSP tine de comportament substituibil: problema este contractul `fly()` stricat, nu taxonomia.

text.en: `fly()` should have been non-virtual.
text.ro: `fly()` ar fi trebuit sa fie ne-virtuala.

explanation.en: Making it non-virtual would not help — the real fix is to not put `fly()` on `Bird` at all, and split out a `BirdThatCanFly` subtype.
explanation.ro: Sa o faci ne-virtuala nu ar ajuta — solutia reala este sa nu pui deloc `fly()` pe `Bird` si sa extragi un subtip `BirdThatCanFly`.

question.en: `Computer` takes an `Input*` in its constructor instead of holding a concrete `Keyboard` member. Which principle does this follow, and what does it enable?
question.ro: `Computer` primeste un `Input*` in constructor in loc sa tina un membru `Keyboard` concret. Ce principiu urmeaza asta si ce permite?

text.en: Single Responsibility — it gives `Computer` only one job.
text.ro: Responsabilitatea Unica — ii da lui `Computer` o singura sarcina.

explanation.en: SRP is about reasons to change. Depending on an interface rather than a concrete type is Dependency Inversion.
explanation.ro: SRP tine de motivele de schimbare. A depinde de o interfata in loc de un tip concret este Inversiunea Dependentelor.

text.en: Liskov Substitution — it lets a `Mouse` replace a `Keyboard`.
text.ro: Substitutia Liskov — permite unui `Mouse` sa inlocuiasca un `Keyboard`.

explanation.en: LSP is a constraint subtypes must satisfy. The act of depending on the abstraction rather than the concrete class is DIP; LSP just makes the substitution safe.
explanation.ro: LSP este o constrangere pe care subtipurile trebuie sa o satisfaca. Actul de a depinde de abstractizare in loc de clasa concreta este DIP; LSP doar face inlocuirea sigura.

text.en: Dependency Inversion — the high-level `Computer` depends on the `Input` abstraction, which makes it testable with a fake `Input`.
text.ro: Inversiunea Dependentelor — `Computer` de nivel inalt depinde de abstractizarea `Input`, ceea ce il face testabil cu un `Input` fals.

explanation.en: Correct. Both `Computer` and the concrete inputs depend on `Input`; a test can pass a `FakeInput`, so no real hardware is needed.
explanation.ro: Corect. Atat `Computer` cat si input-urile concrete depind de `Input`; un test poate trimite un `FakeInput`, deci nu este nevoie de hardware real.

text.en: Open-Closed — it prevents `Computer` from ever being recompiled.
text.ro: Deschis-Inchis — impiedica `Computer` sa fie vreodata recompilat.

explanation.en: OCP is a related benefit, but the specific principle that names "depend on abstractions, not concretions" is Dependency Inversion.
explanation.ro: OCP este un beneficiu inrudit, dar principiul specific care spune "depinde de abstractizari, nu de concretizari" este Inversiunea Dependentelor.

question.en: A single `Animal` interface declares `eat()`, `swim()`, and `fly()`. Writing a `Dog` class, the compiler forces you to implement `fly()`. Which principle is violated, and what is the fix?
question.ro: O singura interfata `Animal` declara `eat()`, `swim()` si `fly()`. Scriind o clasa `Dog`, compilatorul te forteaza sa implementezi `fly()`. Ce principiu este incalcat si care este solutia?

text.en: Interface Segregation — split the fat interface into small ones so `Dog` implements only what it does.
text.ro: Segregarea Interfetelor — imparte interfata grasa in unele mici, ca `Dog` sa implementeze doar ce face.

explanation.en: Correct. ISP says a class must not be forced to depend on methods it does not use; many small interfaces let `Dog` pick only `Animal` and `AnimalThatCanSwim`.
explanation.ro: Corect. ISP spune ca o clasa nu trebuie fortata sa depinda de metode pe care nu le foloseste; multe interfete mici lasa `Dog` sa aleaga doar `Animal` si `AnimalThatCanSwim`.

text.en: Single Responsibility — the `Animal` interface has too many methods.
text.ro: Responsabilitatea Unica — interfata `Animal` are prea multe metode.

explanation.en: SRP counts the reasons a class changes, not the methods on an interface. Being forced to depend on unused methods is specifically ISP.
explanation.ro: SRP numara motivele pentru care o clasa se schimba, nu metodele de pe o interfata. A fi fortat sa depinzi de metode nefolosite tine specific de ISP.

text.en: Liskov Substitution — a `Dog` cannot substitute for an `Animal`.
text.ro: Substitutia Liskov — un `Dog` nu poate inlocui un `Animal`.

explanation.en: A faked `fly()` would later also cause an LSP problem, but the root violation here — a class forced to implement an irrelevant method — is ISP.
explanation.ro: Un `fly()` falsificat ar cauza mai tarziu si o problema LSP, dar incalcarea de baza aici — o clasa fortata sa implementeze o metoda irelevanta — este ISP.

text.en: Open-Closed — adding `fly()` modifies the `Animal` interface.
text.ro: Deschis-Inchis — adaugarea lui `fly()` modifica interfata `Animal`.

explanation.en: OCP is about extending behaviour without editing tested code. The problem here is a class forced to implement methods it does not need — ISP.
explanation.ro: OCP tine de extinderea comportamentului fara a modifica cod testat. Problema aici este o clasa fortata sa implementeze metode de care nu are nevoie — ISP.

question.en: The GoF catalogue splits patterns into three categories. Into which category does Builder fall, and why?
question.ro: Catalogul GoF imparte pattern-urile in trei categorii. In ce categorie intra Builder si de ce?

text.en: Structural — it composes objects into larger structures.
text.ro: Structural — compune obiecte in structuri mai mari.

explanation.en: Structural patterns (Adapter, Composite) are about composition of existing objects. Builder is about constructing one object.
explanation.ro: Pattern-urile structurale (Adapter, Composite) tin de compozitia obiectelor existente. Builder tine de construirea unui obiect.

text.en: Behavioral — it defines communication between objects.
text.ro: Comportamental — defineste comunicarea intre obiecte.

explanation.en: Behavioral patterns (Observer, Visitor) coordinate how objects interact. Builder does not — it assembles one object.
explanation.ro: Pattern-urile comportamentale (Observer, Visitor) coordoneaza cum interactioneaza obiectele. Builder nu — el asambleaza un obiect.

text.en: It is not a GoF pattern.
text.ro: Nu este un pattern GoF.

explanation.en: Builder is one of the original 23 GoF patterns, in the creational group.
explanation.ro: Builder este unul dintre cele 23 de pattern-uri GoF originale, in grupul creational.

text.en: Creational — it is about object creation mechanisms.
text.ro: Creational — tine de mecanismele de creare a obiectelor.

explanation.en: Correct. Builder, Factory, and Singleton are all creational: they control how objects are constructed.
explanation.ro: Corect. Builder, Factory si Singleton sunt toate creationale: controleaza cum sunt construite obiectele.

question.en: Which two pieces, combined, give the Singleton pattern its "only one instance" guarantee?
question.ro: Care doua piese, combinate, ii dau pattern-ului Singleton garantia de "o singura instanta"?

text.en: A `const` constructor and a global variable.
text.ro: Un constructor `const` si o variabila globala.

explanation.en: There is no such thing as a `const` constructor, and a plain global gives no control over creation — that is the very thing Singleton improves on.
explanation.ro: Nu exista asa ceva ca un constructor `const`, iar o globala obisnuita nu da control asupra crearii — exact lucrul pe care Singleton il imbunatateste.

text.en: A private constructor (blocks external `new`) and a static accessor that creates the instance once.
text.ro: Un constructor privat (blocheaza `new`-ul extern) si un accesor static care creeaza instanta o singura data.

explanation.en: Correct. The private constructor stops anyone else from constructing the object; the static `GetInstance()` is the single controlled creation point.
explanation.ro: Corect. Constructorul privat opreste pe oricine altcineva sa construiasca obiectul; `GetInstance()` static este singurul punct de creare controlat.

text.en: A virtual destructor and a friend function.
text.ro: Un destructor virtual si o functie prietena.

explanation.en: Neither is part of the Singleton mechanism. The guarantee comes from a private constructor plus a static accessor.
explanation.ro: Niciuna nu face parte din mecanismul Singleton. Garantia vine dintr-un constructor privat plus un accesor static.

text.en: A static array and a `#define`.
text.ro: Un tablou static si un `#define`.

explanation.en: That describes the MAX_INSTANCES **variant**, which allows several instances. The core Singleton needs only the private constructor + static accessor.
explanation.ro: Asta descrie **varianta** MAX_INSTANCES, care permite mai multe instante. Singleton-ul de baza are nevoie doar de constructorul privat + accesorul static.

question.en: You are constructing one `HttpRequest` object that has many optional fields — headers, body, timeout, retries, auth. Which pattern fits best?
question.ro: Construiesti un singur obiect `HttpRequest` care are multe campuri optionale — antete, corp, timeout, reincercari, autentificare. Ce pattern se potriveste cel mai bine?

text.en: Factory — because the result type might vary.
text.ro: Factory — deoarece tipul rezultatului ar putea varia.

explanation.en: The type is fixed (`HttpRequest`); only the configuration is complex. Factory solves "which class?", not "how to assemble this one?".
explanation.ro: Tipul este fix (`HttpRequest`); doar configurarea este complexa. Factory rezolva "ce clasa?", nu "cum asamblez aceasta instanta?".

text.en: Singleton — so only one request exists.
text.ro: Singleton — ca sa existe o singura cerere.

explanation.en: There is no reason to limit requests to one instance; the problem is assembling a complex object, not capping instances.
explanation.ro: Nu exista niciun motiv sa limitezi cererile la o instanta; problema este asamblarea unui obiect complex, nu limitarea instantelor.

text.en: Builder — assemble the object step by step with named, order-independent calls.
text.ro: Builder — asambleaza obiectul pas cu pas cu apeluri cu nume, independente de ordine.

explanation.en: Correct. Many optional fields is the textbook Builder case; it avoids the unreadable telescoping constructor.
explanation.ro: Corect. Multe campuri optionale este cazul de manual pentru Builder; evita constructorul telescopic ilizibil.

text.en: Adapter — to convert the request interface.
text.ro: Adapter — pentru a converti interfata cererii.

explanation.en: Adapter bridges incompatible interfaces; there is no interface mismatch here, just a complex construction.
explanation.ro: Adapter face puntea intre interfete incompatibile; aici nu exista nepotrivire de interfata, doar o constructie complexa.

question.en: In the Composite pattern, why can a client call `Paint()` on the root of a UI tree without checking whether each node is a leaf or a container?
question.ro: In pattern-ul Composite, de ce poate un client apela `Paint()` pe radacina unui arbore de interfata fara sa verifice daca fiecare nod este o frunza sau un container?

text.en: Leaves and containers expose the same interface; each container forwards `Paint()` to its children, each leaf just paints itself.
text.ro: Frunzele si containerele expun aceeasi interfata; fiecare container trimite `Paint()` mai departe copiilor sai, fiecare frunza doar se deseneaza.

explanation.en: Correct. Uniform treatment of individual objects and compositions is the defining property of Composite.
explanation.ro: Corect. Tratamentul uniform al obiectelor individuale si al compozitiilor este proprietatea definitorie a lui Composite.

text.en: The client downcasts each node with `dynamic_cast` to find out its real type.
text.ro: Clientul face downcast la fiecare nod cu `dynamic_cast` ca sa-i afle tipul real.

explanation.en: The whole point of Composite is to avoid type-checking. Needing `dynamic_cast` would mean the pattern was not applied.
explanation.ro: Tot scopul lui Composite este sa evite verificarea de tip. Nevoia de `dynamic_cast` ar insemna ca pattern-ul nu a fost aplicat.

text.en: Containers have no children, so `Paint()` is always a single call.
text.ro: Containerele nu au copii, deci `Paint()` este mereu un singur apel.

explanation.en: Containers do have children — that is what makes them containers. `Paint()` recurses through the whole subtree.
explanation.ro: Containerele au copii — exact asta le face containere. `Paint()` recursioneaza prin tot subarborele.

text.en: The root is a Singleton, so there is only one node.
text.ro: Radacina este un Singleton, deci exista un singur nod.

explanation.en: Composite is about a tree of many nodes; instance count is unrelated.
explanation.ro: Composite tine de un arbore cu multe noduri; numarul de instante nu are legatura.

question.en: The Visitor pattern is easy to extend along one axis and painful along the other. Which is which?
question.ro: Pattern-ul Visitor este usor de extins pe o axa si dureros pe cealalta. Care e care?

text.en: Adding a new element type is cheap; adding a new operation is expensive.
text.ro: Adaugarea unui tip de element nou este ieftina; adaugarea unei operatii noi este scumpa.

explanation.en: That is the trade-off of putting operations as methods on the elements — the exact thing Visitor is designed to reverse.
explanation.ro: Acela este compromisul punerii operatiilor ca metode pe elemente — exact lucrul pe care Visitor este proiectat sa-l inverseze.

text.en: Both directions are cheap — Visitor has no trade-off.
text.ro: Ambele directii sunt ieftine — Visitor nu are niciun compromis.

explanation.en: Every pattern has a trade-off. Visitor's is precisely that new element types are expensive.
explanation.ro: Fiecare pattern are un compromis. Al lui Visitor este exact ca tipurile noi de element sunt scumpe.

text.en: Both directions are expensive — Visitor should be avoided.
text.ro: Ambele directii sunt scumpe — Visitor ar trebui evitat.

explanation.en: Visitor is excellent when operations grow and elements are stable. It is not to be avoided — it is to be applied on the right axis.
explanation.ro: Visitor este excelent cand operatiile cresc iar elementele sunt stabile. Nu trebuie evitat — trebuie aplicat pe axa corecta.

text.en: Adding a new operation is cheap (one new visitor class); adding a new element type is expensive (every visitor must change).
text.ro: Adaugarea unei operatii noi este ieftina (o clasa visitor noua); adaugarea unui tip de element nou este scumpa (fiecare visitor trebuie sa se schimbe).

explanation.en: Correct. Visitor relocates the cost of change onto the element-types axis — use it only when that hierarchy is stable.
explanation.ro: Corect. Visitor muta costul schimbarii pe axa tipurilor de element — foloseste-l doar cand acea ierarhie este stabila.

question.en: A logging service, an email notifier, and a mobile app all need to react when an order is placed. The order code must not know about any of them. Which pattern, and how does the message travel?
question.ro: Un serviciu de logare, un notificator de email si o aplicatie mobila trebuie toate sa reactioneze cand este plasata o comanda. Codul comenzii nu trebuie sa stie despre niciunul. Ce pattern si cum calatoreste mesajul?

text.en: Chain of Responsibility — the notification is relayed until the first handler consumes it.
text.ro: Chain of Responsibility — notificarea este transmisa pana cand primul handler o consuma.

explanation.en: Chain stops at the first handler — here all three must react. That requires a broadcast, i.e. Observer.
explanation.ro: Chain se opreste la primul handler — aici toti trei trebuie sa reactioneze. Asta cere un broadcast, adica Observer.

text.en: Observer — the order is the subject; it broadcasts one notification to every registered observer.
text.ro: Observer — comanda este subiectul; difuzeaza o notificare catre fiecare observator inregistrat.

explanation.en: Correct. Observer is a one-to-many broadcast: all three observers react, and the subject knows only the `Observer` interface.
explanation.ro: Corect. Observer este un broadcast unu-la-multi: toti cei trei observatori reactioneaza, iar subiectul cunoaste doar interfata `Observer`.

text.en: Adapter — to convert the order interface for each service.
text.ro: Adapter — pentru a converti interfata comenzii pentru fiecare serviciu.

explanation.en: There is no interface mismatch to bridge; the need is to notify many listeners of a state change.
explanation.ro: Nu exista nicio nepotrivire de interfata de rezolvat; nevoia este de a notifica mai multi ascultatori despre o schimbare de stare.

text.en: Visitor — each service visits the order.
text.ro: Visitor — fiecare serviciu viziteaza comanda.

explanation.en: Visitor adds operations over a stable element hierarchy. The problem here is event notification to many listeners — Observer.
explanation.ro: Visitor adauga operatii peste o ierarhie de elemente stabila. Problema aici este notificarea de evenimente catre multi ascultatori — Observer.
